---
title: "Introduction"
---

Tiny DSA is a stylized Python reimplementation of the source Excel workbook. It projects a country’s general-government debt-to-GDP ratio over a five-year horizon under a baseline macroeconomic and fiscal path and one configurable shock. The package is intentionally minimal: it applies a single public-debt accounting identity recursively for five periods and does not reproduce the indicator-and-threshold structure of operational debt-sustainability frameworks.

Install the package directly from the project repository:

```text
uv add "tiny-dsa @ git+https://github.com/Teal-Insights/py-tiny-dsa"
```

See the [Tiny DSA repository](https://github.com/Teal-Insights/py-tiny-dsa) for the latest package and documentation source.

Tiny DSA is intended for domain economists familiar with the standard public-debt accounting identity who need to understand what the model computes, how its inputs and outputs should be interpreted, and where its simplifications depart from operational practice. The debt ratio and primary balance are expressed as percentages of GDP. Real GDP growth and the real interest rate are expressed in percent per annum. The projection is carried out in real terms throughout.

The model deliberately omits:

- inflation’s contribution to the debt ratio;
- exchange-rate dynamics and the currency composition of debt;
- residual financing terms, including stock-flow adjustments and contingent-liability calls; and
- any endogenous response of the primary balance to the macroeconomic environment.

The fiscal stance is exogenous, the snowball factor is computed in real terms, and shocks are step changes to one parameter from a configurable shock year onward. These choices keep the model small enough to trace from inputs to outputs while limiting its realism relative to operational debt-sustainability frameworks.

Tiny DSA is a methodological artifact prepared by Teal Insights. It is not intended for policy use, has not been validated against country-specific data, and is not endorsed by the IMF, the World Bank, or any other institution. The Python package is a reimplementation of the source Excel workbook produced through programmatic extraction, machine translation, and AI-assisted generation. The modeling choices follow standard public-debt accounting literature; the documentation conventions draw on the IMF/World Bank LIC-DSF and IMF FAD Q-CRAFT guidance documents.

The remainder of this documentation describes the package structure and workflow, demonstrates illustrative scenarios, explains the debt-dynamics identity and shock specification, and discusses the realism and limitations of the resulting projections. For the corresponding treatment in operational frameworks, see International Monetary Fund and World Bank (2018), Sections II.B–II.D and Appendix III, and Escolano (2010).

For correctness evidence, see [Excel parity validation](03-excel-parity-validation.qmd), which summarizes the exported-library differential test against the source workbook.
